paragraphs.source_en: When I turned toward the bathroom, the enemy slipped down from the cupboard. When I stood guard over the cupboard, the enemy leapt out again from behind the sink. When I took my stand in the very middle of the kitchen, the enemy began making mischief from all three sides at once. Call it deliberate mischief or call it base tactics; in any case, a gentleman is no match for scoundrels. I ran back and forth a full fifteen or sixteen times, exerting myself with all possible effort, until both mind and body were worn out; yet in the end I did not succeed once. It was most regrettable, but against such petty villains even Admiral Togo, with all his wisdom and valor, would have been helpless. At first I still had courage, a fighting spirit, even a lofty sense of tragic grandeur. But later, after rushing east and west, I felt myself a fool, and being sleepy and exhausted besides, I had no choice but to sit motionless in the middle of the kitchen. Even if I no longer moved, so long as I glared fiercely in every direction, the enemy, being petty creatures, could hardly dare to make too much trouble. When the fellows I had taken for enemies turned out to be unexpectedly mean-spirited creatures, my former sense of glory in war vanished, leaving only the thought that the enemy was hateful. Once that feeling of hatred passed, my spirit slackened, and all that remained was a blank bewilderment. After that stupor, I thought, “Do as you please; after all, you will never amount to anything.” I despised them utterly, and then drowsiness came over me. Having passed through these changes of thought, I at last longed for sleep. I really did fall asleep. It follows that rest is necessary even in the midst of the enemy.

paragraphs.source_en: Another great mass of petals blew in through the skylight that opened sideways toward the eaves. A gust of wind struck my body, and I woke with a start. At that very moment, a creature shot out of the cupboard like an arrow, and before I had time to dodge, it sliced through the air and bit into my left ear. Immediately afterward, another black shadow had scarcely come around behind me before it was hanging from my tail. It all happened in the blink of an eye. I sprang up mechanically, without any clear purpose, concentrating all the strength in my body into my pores as I tried to shake the monster from my tail. The one that had fastened savagely onto my ear lost its balance and dangled beside my face. By chance its tail, soft as a rubber tube, slipped into my mouth. I would not let this chance go; determined to kill it, I clamped hard on that tail and shook my head from side to side until only the tail remained between my front teeth, while its body flew into the wall pasted with old newspapers and rebounded onto the floorboards. I quickly sprang on it just as it was about to get up. Like a ball violently kicked, it swept past the tip of my nose, leapt onto the hanging shelf, and stood there with its legs drawn in. It looked down at me from the shelf; I looked up at it from the floor. The distance between us was about five feet, and between us the moonlight shone sideways like a broad band stretched across the empty air. Putting all my strength into my forelegs, I tried to leap up onto the shelf; my forepaws did manage to catch the edge, but my hind legs were left dangling in the air. The black thing from before was still biting my tail and would not let go. My position was extremely perilous. I shifted my forelegs, trying to get a deeper grip on the shelf, but because of the weight on my tail, each time I changed paws my hold became shallower; if I slipped another two or three tenths of an inch, I would surely fall. I grew more and more endangered, and my claws scratched at the shelf with a rasping, scraping sound. I thought, this will never do. When I shifted my left foreleg, my claws failed completely to catch, and I was left hanging by only my right foreleg. Under the weight of my own body and the weight of the thing biting my tail, my body kept twisting round and round. The monster on the shelf, which until then had remained motionless and fixed its gaze on me, now leapt down at my forehead as though flying. My claws lost their hold all at once, and the three bodies fell together through the moonlight, dragging down the little tub set inside the mortar on the shelf below and an empty jam jar; these fell too, and in turn brought down the fire-extinguishing jar beneath them. Those jars and vessels fell half into the water jar and half onto the floorboards. All of this made an extraordinary racket in the dead of night, chilling even the soul of me as I struggled desperately.

paragraphs.source_zh: 一大堆花瓣又从那向着飞檐横开着的天窗吹了进来。一阵风吹打在我的身上，我猛地惊醒。就在这时，从壁橱里猛地像箭一般窜出来一个家伙，在我还未来得及躲避之前，就嗖地咬住了我的左耳。紧接着又有一个黑影刚奔到我的身后，就马上吊在我的尾巴上了。这完全是一瞬间发生的事。我毫无目的地机械地蹦了起来，把浑身的力量都集中到毛孔上，想把尾巴上的这个怪物甩掉。而那个狠狠咬住我耳朵的家伙失去了重心，在我的脸旁当啷着，想不到它那条像胶皮管一样柔软的尾巴，凑巧进到我的嘴里，我决不放松这个机会，决心弄死它，我狠狠衔住这条尾巴，头左右摇个不停，结果只是一根尾巴留在我的前齿里，它的身子甩到贴有旧报纸的墙上，又反弹在地板上。我趁它正要起来的时候赶紧扑了上去。它像皮球猛地踢过来一样，从我的鼻子尖猛地掠过，跳到吊板上，缩着腿站在那里。它从吊板上向下看着我，我从地板上仰望着它，我和它的距离约有五尺，这中间，月光宛如在虚空张起一条宽幅的带子，横射过来。我用尽前腿力气，想要跳到吊板上，前腿总算抓住了吊板的边缘，但两条后腿却悬空着。刚才那个黑东西死死咬住我的尾巴不放。我的处境十分危急。我换了一下前腿，想要向深里抓住吊板，可是由于尾巴上的重量，我越是倒换前腿，抓得就越浅，再往外滑上两三分，肯定就要掉下来。我越来越危险了，我的爪子挠住吊板，发出“咯吱咯吱”的声音。我想这下子可要坏事。当我倒换左腿的时候，我的爪子一下子没有钩好，只剩下一只右前腿吊在那里。由于我自身的重量加上咬住我尾巴的那个东西的重量，我的身体便来回不停地转悠。在这之前，在吊板上一直一动不动死盯着我的那个怪物，这时朝着我的脑门飞也似的跳了下来。我的爪子一下子失去了抓头，三个物体一齐在月光中掉落下来，带动了放置在下一层吊板上捣罐中的小桶和装果酱的空瓶，它们也跟着一齐坠落了，同时又带动了再下边的消火罐。这些瓶瓶罐罐一半掉进了水缸里，一半掉落在地板上。这一切在深夜里发出了非同寻常的声响，使拼命挣扎着的我为之心胆俱寒。
